title: Building Atlas as a Public Think Tank
description:
Help us build a better way for people to think and solve problems together.
Use this space to examine Atlas itself: what works, what doesn’t, what’s missing, and what could be done differently. Your feedback, problems, and ideas can directly help shape how the public think tank evolves.

title: Solving the Homelessness Crisis
description: Explore why people become or remain homeless, where current responses fall short, and what combinations of housing, services, prevention, treatment, public policy, community support, and other approaches could improve outcomes.

title: What ideas could help make the world better?
description:
An intentionally broad, open-ended inquiry where anyone can contribute an idea they believe could make the world better.
Ideas can be large or small, practical or ambitious, local or global—the point is to create a place for possibilities that people think are worth exploring and building on together.

title: Large homeless encampments and unsheltered homelessness
description: Explore the problems that arise when people live outdoors or in large encampments without stable access to sanitation, safety, storage, shelter, and essential services.

title: Substance use and addiction among people experiencing homelessness
description: Examine how substance use and addiction can contribute to homelessness, how homelessness can make recovery more difficult, and where treatment and support systems fall short.

title: Severe mental illness and lack of consistent treatment
description: Explore the challenges faced by people experiencing homelessness who also live with severe mental illness, especially when consistent treatment, follow-up care, and support are difficult to access or maintain.

title: Lack of affordable and available housing
description: Examine how housing costs, limited housing supply, low vacancy, income constraints, and other barriers can make stable housing inaccessible or difficult to regain.

title: Difficulty escaping homelessness once someone is on the street
description: Explore the interconnected practical barriers that can make it difficult to regain stability after becoming homeless, including access to identification, communication, transportation, hygiene, employment, banking, addresses, and other everyday necessities.

title: People becoming homeless in the first place
description: Explore the pathways that lead people into homelessness and how earlier intervention might prevent it, including eviction, sudden income loss, family breakdown, domestic violence, and transitions out of institutions or other unstable situations.

title: Fragmented homelessness services
description: Examine how assistance can be spread across different agencies, eligibility systems, locations, schedules, and processes that may be especially difficult to navigate while someone is experiencing homelessness.

title: Create one-stop employment transition centers for people experiencing homelessness
description:
Create accessible places where people experiencing homelessness can get practical support to prepare for, find, and begin work.
The idea is to bring together the kinds of basic resources, preparation, assistance, and connections that can help someone move from living on the street toward employment, rather than requiring them to navigate every barrier separately.

title: Redirecting surplus food helps address the homelessness crisis
description:
Connects the surplus-food idea with the homelessness inquiry by proposing that better recovery and distribution of usable surplus food could help meet some immediate food needs among people experiencing homelessness.
The relationship itself is a claim that can be evaluated, challenged, supported, and developed further.

title: Food safety and liability can complicate surplus food redistribution
description:
Surplus food has to remain safe through storage, pickup, transportation, and delivery.
Food businesses may also hesitate to donate when they are uncertain about handling requirements or potential liability if someone becomes ill.

title: Reliable logistics and timing
description:
Surplus food often becomes available unpredictably and may have a short usable window, while shelters, outreach teams, or individuals need food at particular places and times.
Coordinating pickup, transportation, refrigeration, storage capacity, and delivery quickly enough can be difficult even when plenty of food exists.

title: Use Ranked-Choice Voting in More Elections
description:
Allow voters to rank candidates in order of preference instead of choosing only one. If no candidate initially has enough support to win, lower-ranked candidates can be eliminated and those voters’ next choices counted until a winner is determined.
The approach can reduce spoiler effects and give voters more freedom to support their preferred candidates without relying as heavily on strategic voting.

title: Voters may need time to learn a new ballot system
description:
Switching from choose-one ballots to ranked ballots introduces a learning curve.
Clear ballot design, voter education, and transparent counting rules would be important parts of a successful transition.

title: Adopt ranked-choice voting in local elections first
description: Cities or other local jurisdictions could introduce ranked-choice voting for selected elections, publish clear voter guidance, and evaluate ballot completion, voter understanding, election administration, and public response before broader adoption.

title: Ranked-choice voting could encourage more people to run for office
description:
If ranked-choice voting became more common, candidates outside the usual two-party or establishment pathways might have more reason to enter races because voters could support them without the same spoiler concerns.
A larger candidate pool could give voters more choices and potentially improve the odds that capable people enter public service.

title: Ranked-choice voting can make elections harder to understand
description: Critics may argue that multiple rankings and transfer rounds make the final result less immediately intuitive than a simple plurality count, particularly for voters encountering the system for the first time.

title: Create neighborhood libraries for rarely used tools
description:
Neighbors could share tools and equipment that most people only need occasionally instead of every household buying its own.
A simple local lending system could reduce costs and waste while making useful equipment more accessible.

title: Share simple teaching practices that improve participation
description: When a teacher discovers a small change that substantially improves student participation, make the practice easy for other teachers to understand, adapt, test, and improve rather than leaving useful classroom knowledge isolated.

title: Use simple processes to make meetings shorter
description:
Teams can adopt lightweight meeting practices that reduce unnecessary discussion, clarify decisions, and return time to participants.
Small process improvements can be copied by workplaces, volunteer groups, and community organizations almost anywhere.

title: Make it easier to redirect surplus food
description: Restaurants and other food businesses can use simple, repeatable processes to route safe surplus food toward people or organizations that can use it instead of discarding it.

title: Make public information easier to access across languages
description: Public-facing information can be designed and translated so that people who do not primarily speak the dominant local language can more easily understand services, instructions, opportunities, and decisions that affect them.

title: Design social media to channel attention toward collective problem-solving
description: Explore how social media could be intentionally designed to direct more human attention and participation toward constructive collaboration and solving shared problems.

title: Social media designed for collective problem-solving implemented by Atlas, the public think tank
description: Connects the idea of intentionally designing social media for collective problem-solving with Atlas as one possible implementation of that idea.
